rationale: The buyer is a specific and nameable person — a solo SaaS founder or small-business operator running their own email sending infrastructure — and the pain is financially direct (emails in spam = lost revenue or signups). Willingness to pay scores a 5 because paid substitutes exist (Postmark, Mailgun, GlockApps deliverability monitoring), but they solve adjacent problems rather than the Postmaster Tools onboarding/configuration gap specifically. The service is highly buildable and can run autonomously, but with no responsiveness signal yet and a crowded adjacent market, validate-first is correct before committing to build.
solution_plan: The micro-service is a Google Postmaster Tools setup and monitoring assistant: a one-time onboarding service ($49–99 flat fee) plus an optional monthly monitoring dashboard ($19/mo) that checks domain reputation and alerts the operator when signals drop. The factory builds this as a Claude-driven diagnostic flow — an intake form collects the sending domain, DNS records, and Google Postmaster Tools error screenshots; Claude generates a step-by-step remediation guide specific to that configuration; a simple page + Stripe handles payment. Sell to founders in IndieHackers, /r/SaaS, and the MicroConf Slack — all places where solo operators managing their own email stack congregate; outreach goes out only after Youval approves the batch. Delivery is automated: Claude processes the intake form, generates the remediation doc, and sends it via email; the monitoring dashboard pings Google's Postmaster Tools API daily and sends a summary. Youval's only recurring touch is approving outreach batches and reviewing any edge-case support escalations Claude flags as uncertain. This is genuinely buildable by the factory in a week for the MVP — the main risk is that Postmaster Tools issues are often a one-time fix, which limits recurring revenue potential.
notes: operational_autonomy meets the 7 floor; all build gates are at or above minimums. Held at validate due to low responsiveness signal and thin evidence of recurring purchase intent beyond a one-time fix. A small outreach test (20–30 messages in IndieHackers) would confirm willingness to pay quickly.
